subject: Pathology
summary: Left ventricular hypertrophy (LVH) is the thickening of the left ventricular wall due to chronic pressure or volume overload. It alters myocardial structure, reduces compliance, and predisposes to arrhythmias and heart failure.

sections.p: LVH is defined by increased left ventricular mass or wall thickness on imaging or ECG. Diagnosis combines clinical context, imaging, and ECG criteria.
b: Increased LV mass >115 g/m² (men) or >95 g/m² (women) on echo or MRI

t.b: Measures wall thickness and mass; a value above normal indicates LVH and helps stage severity.
Detects voltage criteria for LVH; positive findings support but are less sensitive than imaging.
Gold standard for mass measurement; used when echo is inconclusive or for precise staging.

sections.p: LVH is staged by wall thickness and mass, correlating with risk of complications.

t.b: Determines stage; higher thickness predicts arrhythmia risk.

sections.p: The most common drivers are chronic pressure overload from hypertension and aortic stenosis, followed by volume overload from valvular regurgitation.

t.b: Elevated systolic pressure indicates pressure overload; treat to reduce LVH.
Identifies valvular lesions causing volume or pressure overload.

sections.p: Patients may be asymptomatic or present with exertional dyspnea, chest pain, palpitations, or syncope.

t.b: Detects arrhythmias; presence of atrial fibrillation or ventricular ectopy suggests advanced LVH.

sections.p: Investigations confirm LVH, assess cause, and evaluate complications.

t.b: Measures wall thickness, mass, and valve function; identifies cause and severity.

sections.p: LVH can lead to heart failure, arrhythmias, sudden cardiac death, and ischemia.

t.b: Reduced relaxation predicts heart failure risk.
Detects ventricular ectopy; frequent ectopy raises sudden death risk.

sections.p: Treat underlying cause, control blood pressure, and use drugs that reduce afterload and improve diastolic function.
b: Lifestyle: salt restriction, weight control, exercise

t.b: Reduces afterload, slows LVH regression, and improves survival.

Used if dyslipidemia present; reduces atherosclerotic risk.

sections.p: Regular monitoring of blood pressure, ECG, and echocardiography is essential to track regression and detect complications.

t.b: Maintaining target BP slows LVH progression.
Detects new arrhythmias early.

sections.p: LVH can be mistaken for left ventricular dilation or hypertrophic cardiomyopathy.
ECG voltage criteria may be normal in obese patients or high in athletes; imaging is needed for confirmation.

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden chest pain or shortness of breath

faq.a: Yes, with treatment of the underlying cause and blood pressure control, LV mass can regress.
Many patients are asymptomatic; symptoms appear when complications develop.

faq.q: What is the most common cause of LVH?
faq.a: Hypertension is the leading cause worldwide.

exam: Explain how chronic hypertension leads to LVH and its clinical consequences.
Describe the diagnostic criteria for LVH on ECG and echocardiography.
Outline the first‑line pharmacologic treatment for LVH secondary to hypertension and justify its use.
